title: Drain a source you were handed, closing it with Java 9's try (source)

blocks.text: Since Java 9, a try-with-resources statement can manage a resource that already exists, as long as the variable holding it is final or effectively final: `try (source) { ... }`.
Write `Drain.readAll(LineSource source)`. The source is already open when you get it. Read lines with `readLine()` until it returns `null`, return them in order, and close the source when done.

rows: `["a", "", "b"]` (an empty line is still a line)

blocks.text: The caller handed over the source, so closing it is now your job on every path, whatever a read throws, and every exception, from reading or from closing, reaches the caller. When a read and the close both fail, the read's exception is the one thrown, with the close's added to it as suppressed, as try-with-resources does.

cases.says: It returns every line up to the end and closes the source.
When a read throws, the source is still closed and the read failure reaches the caller.
A failure to close is an IOException like any other: it reaches the caller instead of being swallowed.
When reading and closing both fail, the read failure is thrown with the close failure suppressed into it, not replaced by it.

concepts: Since Java 9, a resource created before the statement can be named in its header with try (res).
